Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei makes it clear to Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and all other companies who signed the open letter in Chinese AI models: We are not for ban, but ...
Article Text:
Anthropic’s Position: not for ban, but…



Keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands

Stopping industrial-scale distillation, where smaller models are trained using outputs from larger ones

Requiring safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, whether open or closed

Read Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s complete post here



A post by Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO

Over the last few days there has been a lot of discussion about open-weights models, especially those from China. Reports suggest that some US officials are considering banning the use of Chinese open-weights models by US companies. In response, many tech companies have signed a letter supporting open-weights models, and some people have even accused Anthropic of wanting to ban open-weights models as a means of protecting our business. Anyone who has read my past writing should know that I don’t regard such bans as a useful measure, but let me state it clearly so that there is no doubt: Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models.

Open-weights models that don’t have dangerous capabilities are a public good: they don’t cost anything besides the compute needed to run them, and they provide value to businesses, developers, and researchers.

Protectionist bans would not address my most serious national security concerns. Specifically, I am worried about two nightmare scenarios. I laid these out in my essay The Adolescence of Technology six months ago1, and have held these positions consistently for many years:

My primary concern is the risk that authoritarian governments—not solely the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), although the CCP is clearly the most capable threat—build AI models that are more powerful than those built by the US, and use them to achieve permanent military superiority or perpetrate incredibly deep repression of their own people. This concern is widely shared within the US government: Vice President

Vance

warned in Paris last year that “authoritarian regimes have stolen and used AI to strengthen their military, intelligence, and surveillance capabilities,” and the Intelligence Community’s 2026 Annual Threat Assessment found that “other global powers’ robust progress in AI is challenging US economic competitiveness and national security advantages.” It is irrelevant whether these models are released with open weights, and certainly irrelevant whether they are used by US businesses. In fact, the most dangerous model may be one that is trained in secret and handed only to the People’s Liberation Army for use in drones and the Ministry of State Security for surveillance and repression.

My secondary concern is the risk that powerful AI models may be misused to carry out cyberattacks or biological attacks, and may have serious alignment problems. Open-weights models—it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else—do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and once weights are released they cannot be withdrawn2. But banning the use of these models by US businesses does nothing to address this risk, because bad actors are unlikely to be legitimate US businesses. It would protect US AI companies from competition, but that has never been my goal.

To address these concerns, I do support the following three measures, which I and Anthropic have consistently advocated for:

We should not sell powerful chips or chipmaking equipment to China, and we should crack down on the rampant smuggling and workarounds used to obtain access to such chips. China has limited domestic production capacity, and therefore, due to the scaling laws, cannot build more powerful models than the US without US chips. This is the most efficient and direct way to block threat #1, and by hampering the training of models that are out of reach of US law, it also indirectly helps with threat.

We should crack down on industrial-scale distillation operations. Distillation is a much more compute-efficient process than training models from scratch. It allows China to build much better models than its number of chips would ordinarily enable, and thus partially evade chip bans. Distillation does not allow the CCP to obtain equivalent or superior AI capabilities to the US, but it can bring the Chinese frontier to within a few months of the US frontier. It is true that many of the companies carrying out these operations release open-weights models—but the open weights are far less relevant than the fact that the operations are backed by an authoritarian state seeking to overtake the US at the frontier. We should have policy interventions to deter this behavior. A blanket ban on open-weights models is neither the correct remedy nor something we have called for.

All sufficiently capable models, open and closed, should go through mandatory safety testing. The best way to address threat #2 is to just directly test models for cyber, biological, and alignment risks before release. I think this idea is actually close to a consensus: I have been heartened both that the

Trump

administration has moved in this direction in recent months, and by recent industry proposals that would apply such testing to the most capable models regardless of their country of origin or whether they are open or closed (while exempting less capable models, such as those from startups and academia, entirely). Whether open models do or don’t pose an increased risk, and whether that risk can be mitigated, is something that should emerge from testing, rather than be decided in advance—and there may be promising methods for improving the safety of open-weights models, including recent research from Anthropic on modular training strategies. Note that to be effective, testing would need to be global, which means even the CCP would need to be on board. I think this may actually be possible: as I wrote in The Adolescence of Technology, limited cooperation around preventing AI biological weapons may be possible because it is in China’s interest too.

This brings me to the open letter. I agree with much of it: open weights expand access to the AI economy, they strengthen competition at least for some use cases, and they give customers greater control. Concerns about distillation should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks—the same measure I described above. But I don’t agree with the letter’s assertions that open-weights models necessarily make it easier to develop safeguards or that broad access to capabilities necessarily helps defenders more than attackers. It seems at least as likely to me that the opposite will be true. For example, I worry that biology will have a strong attacker-defender asymmetry, where sufficiently capable models may be able to quickly weaponize pandemic-level viruses with widely available materials, whereas defense against these agents is a multi-year operational task in the best case (as we saw with Operation Warp Speed)5. Questions like this should be empirically answered by rigorous pre-release testing, not assumed in advance.

To summarize my and Anthropic’s position, we have not and are not advocating for a ban on open-weights models as a category. We should instead focus on keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, stopping industrial-scale distillation, and requiring safety testing of all sufficiently capable models, open and closed.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has sought to clarify his company’s stance amid the growing industry debate over open-weight AI models. In a blog post, Amodei said that Anthropic has “never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” countering criticism that the firm is trying to exert excessive control over the future of artificial intelligence. His comments follow a coalition letter signed last week by Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, Palantir and others, urging policymakers to avoid “premature restrictions” on open-weight models. These models, which users can download, modify, and run independently, have become a flashpoint as Chinese startups dominate the space and US officials weigh possible restrictions.In the post, Amodei said that the real focus should be on:Anthropic previously warned the U.S. Senate about what it described as the “largest known distillation attack” carried out by China’s Alibaba against its Claude models.Amodei further added that he agrees with parts of the coalition letter, including that open0weight models expand access, strengthen competition, and also gibe customers greater control. But he disagreed with the claims that open-0wright models inherently favor cyber defenders over attackers or make it easier to develop safeguards. “Protectionist bans would not address my most serious national security concerns,” Amodei wrote, making clear that Anthropic supports targeted legal frameworks rather than blanket restrictions. His remarks highlight the growing divide in the AI industry over how to balance openness, innovation, and security.
Article Summary: A post by Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, on the use of open-weights models in the U.S. He says Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open- weights models. But he does support the following three measures: stopping industrial-scale distillation, keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, and safety testing for all sufficiently capable models.

Article Title: How a case Oracle lost 14 years ago is troubling Microsoft, forcing it to seek a lifeline from UK's Supreme Court
Article Text:
Why Microsoft changed its defence midway through the ValueLicensing case



What happens next in the £270 million Microsoft licence resale case



In 2012, Oracle went to the European Court of Justice to stop people reselling its software licences second-hand. It lost. That judgment, known as UsedSoft, settled a simple idea: once you sell someone a perpetual software licence, you cannot control what they do with it afterwards. Fourteen years on, that ruling is proving to be Microsoft's biggest problem in a London courtroom.Microsoft has now lost twice in a £270 million case brought by UK reseller ValueLicensing, and it is asking the Supreme Court for permission to try again. The Competition Appeal Tribunal ruled in 2025 that reselling and subdividing Microsoft's on-premise licences did not infringe its copyright. Microsoft appealed. On July 7, it lost that too. On July 21, the tribunal granted an extended stay while Microsoft prepares its Supreme Court application, but stopped short of freezing the case entirely.The dispute began in 2021, and not over copyright at all. ValueLicensing claimed Microsoft inserted contractual clauses that pushed customers toward Microsoft 365 subscriptions while stopping them from reselling their perpetual licences, choking off the supply of surplus Office licences.Microsoft contested that, then shifted tack and argued the resale itself was copyright infringement. The tribunal disagreed. So did the Court of Appeal.The appeal judgment was blunt about where Microsoft's logic led. It said the approach "would produce odd results", pointing out that it created a strange split between software sold on CD-ROM, where Microsoft has no control over resale, and everything else. Worse, the judgment noted that under Microsoft's reading, a company could sidestep UsedSoft entirely by simply bundling "some icons or clip art" into a program.The stay is partial. ValueLicensing's disclosure and confidentiality applications will still be heard, likely at a Case Management Conference in September. Tribunal chair Justin Turner KC called it middle ground, weighing wasted costs against the risk of delay. He noted the claimant had already won at first instance and on appeal.ValueLicensing's Jonathan Horley said the company was pleased a full stay was refused and wants to move toward a liability trial quickly. Microsoft has not commented publicly.The stakes go beyond £270 million. A separate class action over similar claims, represented by Alexander Wolfson, could run into billions of pounds. Microsoft's used-licence argument was never only about ValueLicensing.
Article Summary: Microsoft has now lost twice in a £270 million case brought by UK reseller ValueLicensing. The Competition Appeal Tribunal ruled in 2025 that reselling and subdividing Microsoft's on-premise licences did not infringe its copyright. On July 21, the tribunal granted an extended stay while Microsoft prepares its Supreme Court application.

Article Title: How heatwave in Europe is making Europeans understand that why Americans' 'environment choice' makes more sense
Article Text:
Sales surge across the continent



Heat as a public health risk



Cultural mindset changing



Europe’s heatwave has an important lesson for smartphone users across the world



For decades, much of Europe dismissed air conditioning as an unnecessary luxury, whereas Americans embraced it as a standard part of everyday life. But after Western Europe recoded its hottest June on record and another relentless heatwave pushed temperatures above 100°F, Europeans are buying AC units in unprecedented numbers. According to a report by Business Insider, market analysts say the trend is structural, not temporary, signaling a cultural shift toward cooling solutions once seen as wasteful. Residents like Kieron Heath in Essex, England, have changed their minds. After struggling through increasingly hot summers with fans, Heath spent £585 on a portable unit last year. “Once you get one, you realize it was a complete no-brainer,” he told Business Insider. His experience reflects a growing sentiment across Europe: AC is no longer indulgence, but survival.Manufacturers also reported double-digit growth in AC sales across Italy, Spain, France, and Germany. Samsung, Midea, Mitsubishi Electric, and LG all say demand has surged, with some models selling out. Eurovent, the industry’s trade association, expects the momentum to continue, projecting EU household AC units could exceed 100 million by 2030.The shift is driven not just by comfort but by health. EuroMOMO estimated excess deaths across Europe rose from 33,000 in mid-June to more than 45,000 by early July. In England and Wales alone, researchers linked 2,183 deaths to the late June heatwave. “Rising temperatures and more frequent extreme heat events are becoming impossible to ignore,” Eurovent’s Stijn Renneboog said.Europe’s resistance to AC has long been tied to older housing, high electricity costs, and cultural attitudes. Only one in five European households has AC, compared with nine in ten in the U.S. But as heatwaves intensify, Europeans are beginning to understand why Americans see cooling as essential. “The American mindset is, ‘I’m hot, so why would I stay hot?’” Heath said. “Ours has almost been, ‘Well, there is no other choice but to be too hot. ’ That mindset is beginning to change.”In related news, Among other challenges, the deadly heatwave has caused smartphones and other electronic devices to overheat. As a result, many are putting their devices in fridges and freezers to cool them down. But experts say the situation is an important reminder for smartphone users everywhere. According to a report by BBC, Jamie Farnell, who runs Shropshire Phone Repairs, in Wem, said that he was getting “flooded” with repairs of devices with “internal moisture damage”. Farnell believes the damage is a result from smartphones being put in fridges and freezers.“We used to see people putting their phones in rice, which is another common misconception,” he told the publication. “When they get wet you shouldn't put it in rice it doesn't really do anything.”“Now people are seeing these tips where people are putting phones in the fridge or freezer, but it's not safe to do it. If you put it in, there is a risk of moisture that can get in the phone and then when it does dry out the moisture or the condensation turns into water,” Farnell stated before adding that it was an issue he was seeing from customers “both young and old”.
Article Summary: Sales of air conditioning units across Europe have surged. The trend is signaling a cultural shift toward cooling solutions once seen as wasteful. Only one in five European households has AC, compared with nine in ten in the U.S. In England and Wales alone, researchers linked 2,183 deaths to the June heatwave.

Article Title: US Vice President JD Vance on conversation with a young engineer that made him realise that America’s economic problems run deeper than salaries or jobs
Article Text:
US Vice President JD Vance

Engineer’s frustration highlights a larger problem



Immigration and home ownership



AI could worsen inequality



Mark Zandi's 'warning' for Americans



US Vice President JD Vance says that America’s economic challenges go beyond wages and employment, pointing to a deeper crisis of affordability and opportunity. According to a report by Benzinga, speaking on The Joe Rogan Experience, Vance recalled a conversation with a young engineer earning well above average yet still unable to image owning a home. “You make way more money than 75% of people your age… and you think it is like this ridiculous, unachievable objective to have literally what your parents had,” Vance said.For JD Vance, the frustration of the engineer highlights larger problems: even financially successful professionals feel locked out of the middle-class lifestyle their parents enjoyed. He blamed decades of offshoring industrial jobs, reliance on foreign labor, and Wall Street’s dominance over everyday assets for eroding economic security. Rising housing costs, he said, remain the clearest example of how the system is failing.JD Vance further argued that high immigration levels have intensified competition for housing, though he credited tighter broader policies with helping stabilise rents and prices in recent years. Without a realistic path to homeownership, he also warned that more Americans could lose faith in the system. “It’s created a generation of kids who kind of are attracted to socialism,” he told Rogan.The conversation also turned to artificial intelligence. Rogan also raised concerns about jobs being wiped out, but Vance said that the bigger issue is how AI-driven wealth will be distributed. Comparing the moment to the Industrial Revolution, he warned that if gains flow only to a small elite, inequality could deepen. “The fundamental challenge of AI is it’s going to unleash a lot of wealth creation,” Vance said. “But if that wealth creation all goes to some segment of people, you’re going to have communism.”Recently, Moody’s Analytics top economist, Mark Zandi also raised a warning for Americans. Zandi said that America’s stubborn inflation problem is not a mystery but it’s the result of deliberate policy decisions. In a breakdown shared via a post on X (formerly known as Twitter) Zandi noted that inflation has run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target for 64 straight months, with headline inflation at 3.5%. He also wrote that when you ‘net out the inflation tailwinds and headwinds, it’s clear the uncomfortably high inflation is the result of policy choices’. Zandi also said that the Americans are right to view high inflation and the increasing cost of living as their biggest financial challenge, and he argues that the roots of the problem lie in trade and immigration policies that have reshaped the economy.“Most Americans consider persistently high inflation and the resulting higher cost of living their number one financial problem. With good reason: top-line inflation is running no less than 3.5%, well above the Fed’s 2% target. And inflation has been well above target for five years running. The table breaks down last year's inflation and this year's expected inflation into their underlying factors. Netting out the inflation tailwinds & headwinds, it’s clear the uncomfortably high inflation is the result of policy choices,” wrote Zandi.

Article Title: Chip that can give sight to the blind: Former president of Elon Musk's Neuralink invents only treatment that restores human vision and takes it to Europe
Article Text:

How PRIMA works: Chip and smart glasses



Outpacing Silicon Valley rivals to commercialisation



If someone you know has lost their vision, they may soon get their sight back. Science Corp, a brain-computer interface (BCI) company founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak, has launched the commercial rollout of PRIMA, the world’s only treatment proven to restore functional central vision to blind patients. PRIMA has received the official CE mark under the European Union Medical Device Regulation, authorising its commercial availability across 30 European countries.The first commercial surgery is expected to take place soon in Germany, making it the first device from a US brain-implant company to reach patients on a wide commercial scale. According to research recently published by the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), PRIMA restored vision to patients suffering from GA due to AMD, which is said to have affected more than five million people worldwide.The PRIMA system relies on an ultra-thin, subretinal photovoltaic implant that is placed directly under the affected area of the retina without harming existing natural vision. The wireless implant works in tandem with specialised glasses that project near-infrared light into the eye.The chip absorbs the light and converts it into electrical stimulation signals, allowing the brain to process images once again.Interestingly, the glasses even feature a built-in “zoom-in” capability so users can magnify small text.As per the clinical trial results published, a multi-center trial involving 38 patients across 17 sites showed a mean vision improvement of 25.5 letters (more than 5 lines) on a standard eye chart. The product is claimed to restore reading ability in 84% of patients who regained the ability to read letters, numbers and words. About 80% of patients achieved significant visual acuity improvements after 12 months.“For decades, losing central vision to this disease meant losing the ability to read, recognize faces, and ultimately losing independence. There was no viable treatment. Now there is,” the company stated.While Elon Musk’s Neuralink has dominated public attention, Hodak’s Science Corp. has quietly become the second most valuable US brain-implant company and the first to cross the finish line into commercial sales.Unlike experimental trial devices that remain restricted to research labs, PRIMA is filing for country-specific reimbursement plans across Europe to ensure patients can access the treatment affordably.“This is the first in hopefully a long series of commercial products that proceed to advance that horizon, sometimes incrementally, but relentlessly,” said Max Hodak, founder and CEO of Science Corp. In the US, Science Corp. is working closely with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to bring PRIMA to the American market.

Article Title: China ‘threatens’ US over investigation after US government accused Kimi K3 AI model maker Moonshot AI of ‘stealing’ Anthropic's Fable model
Article Text:
America accuses Moonshot AI of ‘distillation’



Sanctions and Entity List threats by the US



China’s Commerce Ministry has warned of countermeasures after American officials threatened sanctions and trade restrictions against Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies over intellectual property (IP) theft allegations. Beijing’s response follows accusations from Washington that Beijing-based AI startup Moonshot AI illegally “distilled” Anthropic’s advanced Claude Fable 5 model to create its newly released Kimi K3 system.Accusing Washington of “AI hegemonism”, China's ministry pushed back, stating that the US is threatening Chinese tech companies without factual or legal grounds, as per a report by news agency Reuters. A ministry spokesperson said: “For any action that causes substantive harm to Chinese interests, China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”Model distillation is a practice where developers use the outputs of a stronger AI model to train or refine a smaller system. However, US officials argue that Moonshot crossed the line from standard training into large-scale extraction and corporate espionage.Last week, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, said that the US government uncovered evidence that Moonshot built a complex internal infrastructure to covertly extract data from Anthropic.The AI company previously reported identifying over 3.4 million interactions linked to Moonshot across hundreds of fraudulent accounts targeting Claude’s reasoning, coding and computer-use capabilities.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned last week that Chinese tech companies conducting illicit distillation could face placement on the Commerce Department’s Entity List or severe financial sanctions.“We support open-source AI and the innovation it unlocks. But open source is not open season on American IP. When PRC firms conduct covert, industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft, sanctions and Entity List designations will be on the table,” Bessent wrote on X (formerly Twitter).Moonshot has denied the accusations, claiming that Kimi K3’s high performance in coding and problem-solving relies on its own proprietary architectural breakthroughs.
Article Summary: China’s Commerce Ministry has warned of countermeasures after American officials threatened sanctions and trade restrictions against Chinese tech companies. Washington accuses Beijing-based AI startup Moonshot AI of illegally ‘distilling’ an advanced Claude Fable 5 model to create its Kimi K3 system.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Oracle founder Larry Ellison: "Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by…" - a powerful lesson on ambition, failure and the mindset behind extraordi
Article Text:
Representative Image

Quote of the day by Oracle founder Larry Ellison

"Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure"

Understand the meaning behind Larry Ellison’s quote

Why fear of failure can actually be useful

Why success on its own is never really enough

Why continuous improvement matters more than any single achievement

Why setbacks often build real resilience

Why discipline tends to outlast raw talent

Why this is not the same as harmful anxiety

Other famous quotes by Larry Ellison

"When you innovate, you've got to be prepared for people telling you that you are nuts."

"Life's a journey. It's a journey about discovering limits."

"The most important aspect of my personality as far as determining my success goes has been my questioning conventional wisdom, doubting experts and questioning authority."

"I have had all the disadvantages required for success."

“Now, most people hate to admit they're wrong, but it didn't bother Bill one bit. All he cared about was what was right, not who was right. That's what makes Bill very, very dangerous.”

What it means in today's world

Most people assume successful individuals are pulled forward purely by ambition, chasing wealth, recognition and big wins. Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle, offered a different explanation for what actually drives people to the top. "Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure," he said. It is not really an argument in favour of fear. It is an observation about where a lot of real discipline actually comes from, and it fits closely with how Ellison himself has described building one of the largest technology companies in the world from a much smaller and far less certain starting point. The quote suggests that lasting success often comes not from comfort or confidence alone, but from using the possibility of failure as motivation to prepare thoroughly, work consistently and keep improving.Most people picture successful individuals as motivated purely by optimism, chasing the next win with total confidence. Ellison is describing something a little different from that picture entirely. Plenty of top performers push themselves relentlessly because they understand exactly what failure would actually cost them, and rather than freezing up over that possibility, they use it to stay sharp and keep improving.The key distinction sitting inside the quote is between fear that stops someone acting at all and fear that pushes someone to prepare properly. The first shuts things down. The second is what actually keeps people sharp long after they could reasonably have relaxed.Fear usually gets treated as something purely negative, and plenty of it is. Not all fear works that way though. A healthy awareness that things could go wrong tends to make people prepare more thoroughly, practise more consistently, and think harder before big decisions. Athletes train hard precisely because they know competition will be demanding. Students revise because exams genuinely require it. In every one of these cases, the possibility of failing is exactly what pushes people to put in more effort, not less.Success has a way of creating comfort, and comfort has a way of turning into complacency. Plenty of people and organisations start declining right after they succeed, simply because they stop pushing once things feel secure. Markets shift. Technology moves on. Customer expectations change constantly. People who stop learning at that point tend to fall behind fairly quickly. Ellison's quote is really arguing that staying aware of the possibility of failure is exactly what keeps great achievers improving, even well after they have already succeeded.Real achievement is rarely the product of one single effort. It usually gets built slowly, through constant refinement, learning new skills, correcting mistakes, adapting when circumstances shift, and continuing to look for better solutions even when the current one already works fine. People who keep this habit up stay ready for whatever comes next, because they never fully stopped asking how they could be a little better than they were yesterday.Failure is rarely pleasant in the moment, yet many successful people describe it afterward as one of the most useful teachers they ever had. A failed product reveals a genuine weakness worth fixing. A rejected idea often leads directly to a better one. Resilience really develops through treating a setback as useful information rather than as a final verdict on someone's ability, which is exactly the alertness Ellison's quote is describing, an ongoing willingness to notice what went wrong instead of simply moving past it without learning anything at all.Natural ability gives someone a head start. Discipline is what actually determines whether that ability gets developed properly over time. Someone genuinely motivated to avoid failure tends to build habits around regular practice, careful preparation and continuous learning, and those habits usually end up mattering more in the long run than raw talent ever did on its own, since talent alone rarely survives the first serious setback without something sturdier underneath it.It is worth being clear about the difference here. Constant anxiety that damages confidence or actively prevents someone from trying anything is not what this quote is describing. Healthy motivation sounds like "I want to prepare properly because this genuinely matters." Unhealthy anxiety sounds like "I should not even try in case I fail." The first pushes someone into action. The second keeps them frozen in place.The pace of change today makes continuous improvement close to essential rather than simply admirable. Skills that mattered five years ago can become outdated surprisingly quickly. Ellison's quote is a reminder that lasting achievement usually depends less on celebrating a past success and more on staying genuinely committed to the next round of improvement. The awareness that failure remains a real possibility is exactly what keeps that commitment alive long after the applause for the last win has faded, which is really the whole difference between a career that keeps growing and one that quietly stalls out.
Article Summary: Larry Ellison: Great achievers are driven not by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure. Ellison's quote suggests that lasting success often comes not from comfort or confidence alone, but from using the possibility of failure as motivation to prepare thoroughly.
